1968 Chevrolet Caprice Station Wagon Sells for Record Price
16 photos
Photo: Mecum Auctions
When it comes to classic cars sold at public auctions, we usually report records set by iconic models, mainly from the high-performance and luxury segments. That's where the big bucks are. But from time to time I like to check the more mundane cars, mostly to observe market trends. Well, I just learned that the 1968 Chevrolet Caprice is now a potentially more valuable classic.
Introduced in 1966, the Caprice was Chevrolet's range-topping model. It sat above the Impala and competed against the Ford LTD, Plymouth Fury VIP, and AMC Ambassador DLP. It had a more upscale interior and a flashier exterior. Sixty years later, the first-generation Caprice is a popular choice for lowrider builders and restomodders, but it's not a highly collectible classic.
While some examples have sold for over $50,000 and even reached into $80,000 territory, they're still far from fetching six-figures (which contemporary Impalas and Corvettes do). In fact, the average auction price for a first-gen Caprice in excellent condition is still under $25,000. And that's precisely why a 1968 Caprice selling for over $80,000 is pretty big news.
It happened at Mecum's Las Vegas 2026 auction on November 13, where a station wagon changed hands for $82,500. Mind you, this isn't an expensive custom fitted with a modern powertrain, but a frame-off restoration completed with new-old-stock components. This thing is as factory-correct as they get.
It looks like it just rolled off the showroom floor, sporting impeccable paint, shiny chrome trim, and outstanding simulated wood panels. It has a matching three-row interior and still relies on the original 327-cubic-inch (5.4-liter) V8 engine.
The price may seem a bit surprising given the lack of a big-block mill, but I should point out that this Caprice is loaded with options and accessories—over 40, to be exact. The list includes the rare stainless upholstery trim, AC, power everything, cruise control , multi-plex stereo, tissue dispenser, and a roof rack. It also has the rare hideaway headlamps.
There is an exception to the factory-correct status I mentioned above: The ad says that the Caprice has a "modified suspension with front and rear air bags."
The selling price makes this station wagon by far the most expensive 1968 Caprice ever sold at public auction; it smashed the previous record by nearly $30K. Up until now, the benchmark was held by a two-door hardtop that sold for $53,900 in early 2023. The same car traded for over $40,000 in 2022 and 2023 again. Before that, the record belonged to a different station wagon that changed hands for $38,000 in 2019.
At the same time, this grocery-getter is now the most expensive first-generation Caprice ever sold at public auction. It smashed a record previously set by a 1966 two-door coupe at $71,500 in 2016.
What's your take on this auction? Is the first-gen Caprice on its way to becoming a more valuable classic, or is this wagon an exception? Would you pay over $80,000 for a long-roof Chevy?
